left_items.title: The decision
left_items.body: Launch the Carry1st Shop in Brazil, Argentina, Mexico, Colombia and Bolivia by Black Friday, 27 November 2026, through a merchant of record: EBANX direct, or EBANX and dLocal through Yuno.

left_items.title: The economics to beat
left_items.body: A $10 average and $5 median ticket, so every fixed fee per transaction is punished; $4 to 5M a month in LatAm by end 2027 (Carry1st, Cordel, Oct 2026, estimate).

left_items.title: What EBANX direct gives
left_items.body: One agreement and one integration for all five countries once EBANX enables each; but one approval rate, one price, Bolivia cash only, no MODO.

left_items.title: What is still open
left_items.body: Volumes by country, EBANX's proposed rates, Carry1st's take rate and the tax treatment under each MoR. Every modeled number in this deck carries its label and an owner.

right_cards.title: One integration, two merchants of record
right_cards.body: EBANX primary, dLocal second, both as connections on the Yuno SDK: retries and failover between them, local methods per market, Phase 2 local acquirers without touching checkout.

right_cards.title: A fee that scales with sales, not with transactions
right_cards.body: $7,500 a month including the first $500K of monthly sales, then 30 / 25 / 20 bps on sales above it. At launch: $7,500 and nothing per transaction; at $4.5M: $18,750 a month, 0.42% of sales.

right_cards.title: A case that pays back in month two
right_cards.body: Base case at run rate: $44.2 per $1,000 of sales through Yuno against $45.0 direct, +$29.1K a month net ($349K a year, 2.6x Yuno's cost); break-even about 65,000 transactions a month.

slides.bottom: Decide by 23 Oct, onboard EBANX and dLocal in parallel, launch Brazil by 27 Nov; the conservative case is cost-neutral at run rate.
slides.source: Yuno business-case model, 15 Oct 2026, base scenario: EBANX direct all-in 4.5% of sales and a 15% take rate are estimates, replaced by EBANX's quote and Shop margins. Volumes: Carry1st, Cordel, Oct 2026, estimate.
slides.notes: The whole deck on one slide. Left, where you stand: five markets, six weeks, a $5 median ticket and a run-rate estimate that is yours. Right, what we propose: one integration carrying EBANX and dLocal, a fee that is a share of what you sell with the first $500K of monthly sales inside the platform fee, and a business case that, in the base scenario, makes the Yuno route the cheaper cost line at run rate before counting approval or coverage gains. Two numbers to keep: break-even at about 65,000 transactions a month, and the conservative case cost-neutral at run rate. Everything modeled is labelled and will be re-cut on your volumes and EBANX's quote.

slides.kicker: WHERE CARRY1ST STANDS · THE SHOP AND THE PLAN
slides.headline: Five markets, a $10 average ticket and six weeks to Black Friday: the launch has to be fast, local and cheap per transaction.

tiles.label: storefronts across Africa, the Middle East and the US: game top-ups and gift cards, instant delivery
average ticket; median about $5 (Carry1st, Cordel, Oct 2026, estimate)

slides.left_note: Founded 2018 in Cape Town; backed by a16z, BITKRAFT, Google, Konvoy and Sony. Publishing partners include Activision, Supercell and EA. The US storefront already lists Free Fire Diamonds (LATAM) and Brazil SKUs.
slides.mid_header: THE LATAM PLAN AS YOU DESCRIBED IT
mid_items: Brazil first, then Argentina, Mexico, Bolivia and Colombia; all five together if payments, localization and support fit in two to three weeks.
Launch through a merchant of record (no LatAm entities today); non-resident accounts and local entities are a Phase 2 decision.
$4 to 5M a month by end 2027 (Carry1st, Cordel, Oct 2026, estimate): about 450,000 transactions a month at a $10 ticket. Volumes by country to come.
slides.right_body: **Live by 27 November 2026.** Local methods that confirm in seconds (Pix, PSE, SPEI, wallets), because the Shop promises instant delivery. **A domestic charge in local currency,** so cards are not declined as cross-border and gamers do not pay FX or foreign-purchase taxes. **One approval rate to beat, not to accept:** a second provider in play from day one. **Spanish and Portuguese** checkout and support. **Costs that scale with a $5 median,** never a fixed fee per transaction.
slides.bar: Six weeks to Black Friday: provider contracts and KYC are the critical path; the Yuno integration itself is measured in days (Yuno estimate, section 07).
slides.source: Discovery call, Oct 2026 (Cordel's figures are estimates, not yet aligned internally); shop.carry1st.com sitemap and Carry1st press releases 2021 to 2026, read 15 Oct 2026.
slides.notes: This is the plan as you described it, in your numbers. We label the run rate as your estimate because you told us it is not yet aligned internally, and the model in this deck runs at four volumes so it holds whichever way the alignment lands. The right-hand column is the checklist we built the launch against: speed, local methods that confirm instantly, domestic presentation of the charge, a second provider from day one, and costs that behave at a $5 median.

slides.kicker: WHERE CARRY1ST STANDS · WHAT THE FIVE MARKETS DEMAND
slides.headline: In every launch market the method that wins is local and instant, and most of it sits outside international card rails.

tiles.label: of Brazil's online purchases are Pix (2025); cards 41%
of Colombia's e-commerce transactions run on PSE (Q2 2025)
of Argentina's e-commerce value is in digital wallets (2024)
of Mexican online buyers pay with debit cards (AMVO 2024)

slides.right_header: WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE SHOP

right_items.title: Instant confirmation is the product
right_items.body: Pix, PSE, SPEI and wallets confirm in seconds, which matches instant top-up delivery. Cash vouchers (Boleto, OXXO, Rapipago) confirm hours or days later and belong in a second wave.

right_items.title: Domestic presentation decides approval
right_items.body: Vendor-reported ranges put cross-border card approval at 30 to 60% against 80 to 90% for local processing (2017 to 2026). A merchant of record charging in local currency is what lets a Brazilian or Mexican debit card approve.

right_items.title: Taxes follow the rail
right_items.body: Argentina adds a 30% perception on foreign-currency card purchases; Brazil charges 3.5% IOF on international card payments. A local-currency charge through the MoR's local entity is domestic for the gamer. TO VALIDATE with EBANX and dLocal.

right_items.title: Bolivia and Argentina need a second provider
right_items.body: EBANX lists only PagosNet cash in Bolivia and no MODO or interoperable QR in Argentina; dLocal carries cards, QR and MODO there.

slides.bar: The Shop's African playbook, local methods in local currency, is exactly what LatAm requires; the open question is which rail carries it.
slides.source: Reuters on PCMI data, 10 Feb 2026; CCCE via Valora Analitik, 24 Aug 2025; PCMI 2024 data; AMVO Estudio 2024; approval ranges are vendor-reported (Worldline, Rapyd, Nuvei, Antom, EBANX, 2017 to 2026); ARCA RG 5617/2024; Decree 12.499/2025. PUBLIC DOCS.
slides.notes: Four numbers, one per market, and they point the same way: the winning method is local and it confirms instantly. Pix in Brazil, PSE in Colombia, wallets in Argentina and debit cards in Mexico are the rails the Shop needs on day one. The approval ranges on the right are vendor claims, not independent studies, so we show them as ranges and label them; the direction is not in dispute. The two tax lines explain why a local-currency charge through a merchant of record matters for the gamer, and both are items we will confirm in writing with EBANX and dLocal.

slides.notes: We start with the honest answer to your question. One EBANX integration and one agreement can switch on all five countries: the country is a field in the request, and EBANX enables each country on your account during onboarding, with sandbox tests per country and an integration review before production. The middle column shows what it costs to fix that with a second direct build. The right column is the same fix as a routing rule.

slides.notes: Cordel asked us to make pricing work for small purchases, so here is the same 450,000 transactions at three tickets. A fixed fee is blind to the ticket: five cents is 0.5% of a $10 sale and 1% of a $5 sale, ten cents twice that. Yuno's usage is a share of what you sell, so on a $5 purchase the marginal cost is one to one and a half cents, and all-in at run rate 0.57% of sales. We are upfront about the one fixed element: at launch volume and a $5 ticket the platform fee alone is 3% of sales, and the structure earns its keep as volume ramps rather than in month one.

slides.notes: The proposal in one slide. A flat platform fee of $7,500 a month that already covers the first $500K of monthly sales, and above that a share of what you sell: 30 basis points to $3M, 25 to $6M, 20 above, each band on the volume inside it, only on approved payments, never a fee per transaction. At launch you pay the platform fee and nothing else; at the $4.5M run rate the all-in cost is $18,750 a month, 0.42% of sales, about four cents on a $10 purchase. Orchestration, smart routing, Monitors, the vault, the dashboard and a dedicated team are inside the platform fee; network tokens and 3DS are billed on usage and quoted separately.

slides.headline: A merchant of record launches in weeks, local presence in months; through Yuno the move happens without a rebuild.

slides.notes: Fatih asked for merchant of record against local presence with launch time and the long-term customer experience. The short version: the MoR launches in weeks and gives the gamer a domestic charge in local currency from day one; a local entity takes months and pays off at scale through lower processing and local acquiring. The Yuno column is the point: because the acquirer is a connection, Carry1st can make that move in Brazil first and Mexico second without touching the checkout, and keep the MoR live as fallback while it does.
